source_read: PMC HTML (PMC3600438; the published PNAS reply, 110(11):E980-E982, not an author manuscript), read in full on 2026-10-31: all five text paragraphs, figure captions, footnotes. Figs. 1-3 not inspected: the browser pane was hidden (the page reported itself hidden) and screenshots came back blank, so values and any sample sizes printed only on the figures are unchecked.

claims.overstatement: Slight: 'did not predict adolescent-onset dependence' drops 'significantly'. The source reports a non-significant test (chi-square 1.15, P = 0.56) in a small group, which is not the same as no association. For IQ change, 'did not predict' is fair (r = −0.006 in the full cohort).
claims.note: All four coefficients check against the text: −0.152 (t −4.45, P < 0.0001; the published sex-adjusted model), −0.158 with SES (t −4.58), −0.151 with childhood self-control (t −4.38, P = 0.0001), and −0.155 in middle-class families only (t −3.61, P = 0.0003). Chi-square 1.15, P = 0.56 and r = −0.006 also check; P = 0.86 is not in the claim. Consistency checks: P = 0.56 matches a chi-square of 1.15 on 2 df (three SES groups), and r = −0.006 with about 870 people gives P of about 0.86. Not checked: the 553 people from middle-class families. That number is not in the text and must come from Fig. 2 or 3, which I could not view. A rough check from the printed beta and t (n ≈ 550 after scaling to the full-sample values) makes it plausible. Not stated in the source: whether beta is standardized. Points the claim could carry: SES and self-control were each added alone, never together or with the other dependence covariates; the middle-class analysis excludes high- as well as low-SES families; SES is the breadwinner's occupation; the reply shows no IQ trajectories before use by exposure group (Fig. 1 is IQ by SES); and the authors' wording ('actual data exclude the possibility', 'these tests exclude') is stronger than single-covariate adjustment allows. The claim does not repeat that wording.

anchors.extracted: In the Dunedin cohort, low SES did not significantly predict adolescent-onset cannabis dependence (chi-square 1.15, P = 0.56); 23% of the adolescent users came from low-SES families (low-skill occupations of the breadwinner).

anchors.locator: Reply text, 3rd paragraph (second point); Fig. 1 caption
anchors.extracted: IQ of children from low-SES families did not change from school entry to adolescence or from adolescence to adulthood (citing a 1993 Dunedin paper; Fig. 1, not viewed); low SES was unrelated to adolescent-to-adult IQ decline, r = −0.006, P = 0.86.

anchors.locator: Reply text, 3rd paragraph (third point); Figs. 2 and 3 captions
anchors.extracted: Reported association of persistent cannabis dependence with IQ decline beta −0.152 (t −4.45, P < 0.0001); with SES controlled beta −0.158 (t −4.58, P < 0.0001); restricted to middle-class families, excluding low- and high-SES families, beta −0.155 (t −3.61, P = 0.0003). Captions say the middle-class restriction gave the same pattern by waves of dependence (Fig. 2) and by age of onset (Fig. 3B). No n for the middle-class subsample in the text; figure values not viewed.

Childhood self-control, measured before cannabis use, was unrelated to IQ decline (r = −0.034, P = 0.31); with it controlled, beta −0.151 (t −4.38, P = 0.0001) against −0.152. Daly's own test (National Child Development Study) measured personality at 50, after use, with no age-of-onset or persistence measure.
The authors state that tests more sensitive to SES did not show worse decline, but give no figures for this.

The authors accept that observational studies cannot prove causation and list their design features (prospective order, dose-response, within-person change from childhood, informant reports, exclusion analyses, education). They cite an argument that adjusting for confounders without a theoretical rationale can mislead. Each alternative (SES, self-control) was tested by adding it alone; no joint model is reported.

key_findings.note: The text says 'adolescent cannabis users' for the 23%, which may mean adolescent-onset users; the card's distinction between the two denominators is fair but uncertain.

The text part is confirmed (no change in low-SES children's IQ; r = −0.006, P = 0.86). The text says 'from the beginning of schooling to adolescence', not 'childhood'. The Fig. 1 values (about 94 to 92, 101 to 100, 110 to 110) were not checked: the pane was hidden and screenshots came back blank.

key_findings.correction: Not checked rather than wrong. The text part is confirmed: middle-class families only, excluding low- and high-SES families, beta −0.155, t −3.61, P = 0.0003 (3rd paragraph). The n of 553 and the bar values (about −0.37 against −0.38) appear only on Fig. 2, which I could not view; targeted check needed. A rough back-calculation from beta and t gives an n near 550, so 553 is plausible.

Not checked rather than wrong. The whole finding (group sizes 9/32, 8/10, 17/8 and bar heights) rests on Fig. 3B, which I could not view. The caption confirms only that panel B shows the same pattern as panel A, with no p values. Targeted check needed. If the sizes are right, the middle-class age-of-onset cells total 84.

key_findings.note: Recomputed: t = 4.38 gives two-sided P of about 1.2 × 10^-5, so the printed P = 0.0001 is inconsistent with the t, as the card says.

reporting_issues.note: Occupational examples only (foodpacker; building inspector, aircraft mechanic; dentist); no scale, cut-offs, timing or class sizes.

Not checked rather than wrong. The text part is confirmed: low-SES IQ said not to change 'from the beginning of schooling to adolescence'. The figure detail on which the issue rests (Fig. 1 starts at age 7, with no group sizes or error bars) could not be viewed. Meier et al. (2012) say childhood IQ was tested at 7, 9, 11 and 13, which fits. Targeted check needed.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high, driven by confounding. On the narrow question (do SES as classified or childhood self-control explain the association?), the tests are direct and use measures taken before cannabis use. On the causal question, each covariate is added alone to the sex-only model.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is defensible because the tests are direct and the letter says observational studies cannot prove causation. Even so, the title ('No evidence that ... confound') and the text ('actual data exclude the possibility', 'these tests exclude') claim more than single-covariate adjustment and a three-class occupational SES measure can show; 'moderate' would also be defensible.

missed: The claim built on this reply says SES 'did not predict adolescent-onset dependence'. The source says 'did not significantly predict' (chi-square 1.15, P = 0.56), in a small group: Meier 2012's Fig. 2 has 52 people with dependence before 18. The card could note that the test had little power. That would keep 'no significant association' from being read as 'no association'.
